sections.h2: Which Scioto County offices deal with property tax?
sections.html:
Three county offices share the work, all at 602 7th Street in Portsmouth. The Scioto County Auditor (Room 103, phone 740.355.8264, open 8:00 am to 4:30 pm on weekdays) sets values and takes appeals and homestead applications. The Scioto County Treasurer (Room 102, phone (740) 355-8272) sends the bills and collects the money. The Scioto County Recorder (Room 110) files the deed after the auditor has processed the transfer.

The treasurer's office describes itself as part of the county's check and balance system with the auditor. In practice that means you ask the auditor why a value changed and ask the treasurer what you owe and when.

sections.h2: How much did the latest triennial update change Scioto County values?
sections.html:
The auditor reports that countywide values rose by about 26.4 percent on average in the latest triennial update, which Ohio law requires every three years. The office explains that the Ohio Department of Taxation requires counties to keep an assessment ratio between 90 and 110 percent of market value based on the prior three years of sales, and that rising prices pushed values up to meet that range.

The auditor adds that state reviewers rejected the first set of tentative values and required resubmission using values deemed sufficient for approval. Values come from sales data, market trends and statistical analysis, not from a physical inspection of every house. The average hides wide differences, so open your own parcel record and compare it with recent sales near you.

Farmland owners should know that current agricultural use value rates are reset in a triennial year by the state, not by the auditor.

sections.h2: What is the Inflation Cap Credit on a Scioto County tax bill?
sections.html:
House Bill 186 created an "Inflation Cap Credit" that was applied to qualifying school district levies, and the auditor says it shows as its own line on the bill. The amount depends on parcel-specific data, so it varies from house to house.

  • If you paid your second-half bill before the credit was applied, you need not do anything.
  • Any overpayment carries forward and is applied to the next first-half bill.
  • Homeowners who pay through an escrow account at a lender need no action, according to the treasurer, who said it was working directly with lenders.

The state's implementation work delayed the second-half bills that year. The treasurer moved the due date for second-half real estate and manufactured home taxes to August 20, 2026, and that date has passed.

sections.h2: When are Scioto County property taxes due and what is the penalty?
sections.html:
Ohio law lets an owner pay the full year by December 31, or pay half by then and the other half by June 20 (R.C. 323.12). A payment counts as on time if the treasurer receives it by the last day or if the envelope carries a United States Postal Service postmark on or before that day. A private meter postmark does not count.

The county can move a date, as it did for the 2026 second half. Always read the due date printed on your bill instead of assuming the statutory one.

Late payment rules from R.C. 323.12 and 323.121, Ohio Revised Code
EventWhat the statute says
First half unpaid after its due dateA 10 percent penalty on the unpaid balance of that half
Second half unpaid after its due dateA like 10 percent penalty on the balance of unpaid current taxes
Delinquent taxesInterest at the rate set under R.C. 5703.47, charged on set dates
Valid delinquent tax contract in forceNo interest while the contract stays in effect, and no second-half penalty on the covered current taxes

If you cannot pay, call the treasurer early and ask about a delinquent tax contract before the penalties build.

sections.h2: How do I challenge my Scioto County property value?
sections.html:
File a complaint with the county auditor on or before March 31 of the following tax year, or on the closing date of first-half collection if that is later (R.C. 5715.19). The auditor then presents it to the county board of revision, and a complaint that arrives by mail is dated by its postmark.

The auditor also invites owners who believe the market value is wrong to file a complaint form with supporting evidence. Good evidence includes:

  • a recent appraisal or closing statement for your own home
  • sales of similar nearby houses
  • repair estimates that show a defect lowering value
  • photos or a report of damage from a casualty

A repeat filing has a limit. Within the same interim period, you may not file against the same parcel again unless the property sold in an arm's length sale, lost value through a casualty, gained a substantial improvement, or saw occupancy shift by at least fifteen percent.

sections.h2: Who qualifies for the Scioto County homestead exemption?
sections.html:
The Scioto County Auditor's page says the state-funded exemption is open to a homeowner who is at least 65 during the first filing year, or permanently and totally disabled, who owns and lives in the home as a principal residence on January 1 of the filing year and who meets state income limits. Separate applications exist for persons 65 or older, for disabled persons, for veterans, and for surviving spouses of public service officers killed in the line of duty.

The applicant's name must be on the deed, and only one application is allowed per property. A reduction, if granted, shows on the bill received the following January. A surviving spouse can qualify between ages 59 and 65 under conditions the page lists. Call 355-8224 or stop in at Room 103 for forms.

sections.h2: How are Scioto County taxes handled when I sell the house?
sections.html:
Ask the Scioto County Treasurer for a payoff on the parcel, including any delinquent amount, before you accept an offer. The title company uses that figure to set aside tax money from your proceeds at closing. The deed then goes through the auditor, who endorses the conveyance, and on to the recorder.

A homestead reduction belongs to the qualifying owner. The auditor's page says changes in ownership must be reported, and the statement of value the buyer files under R.C. 319.202 asks the seller whether the property receives a tax reduction or an agricultural-use valuation. It also carries a notice to the buyer about eligibility for the reduction.

sections.h2: What does the Census Bureau show about the Scioto County housing market?
sections.html:
QuickFacts for Scioto County reports 3,949 veterans, 20.6 percent of residents at age 65 or older and 89.8 percent of people living in the same house a year earlier. Only 10 building permits were issued in 2025, and the mean commute is 27.9 minutes. Among adults 25 and older, 88.8 percent finished high school and 18.2 percent hold a bachelor's degree or more.

Owners lived in 68.4 percent of homes in 2020 to 2024, at a median value of $137,900. A county with this many residents past 65 has a lot of potential homestead filers, so the program is worth checking before you list.

faqs.q: When are Scioto County property taxes due?
faqs.a: Ohio law sets December 31 for the first half and June 20 for the second. The county moved the second-half 2026 date to August 20, and that date has passed. Check the date printed on your own bill.

faqs.q: Who sends the property tax bill in Scioto County?
faqs.a: The Scioto County Treasurer, at 602 7th Street, Room 102, Portsmouth, phone (740) 355-8272. The auditor sets the value, and the treasurer bills and collects the tax.

faqs.q: What is the deadline to file a valuation complaint in Scioto County?
faqs.a: A complaint is filed with the county auditor by March 31 of the following tax year, or the closing date of first-half collection if that is later. The board of revision then hears it.

faqs.q: What penalty applies if I pay late?
faqs.a: Ohio charges a 10 percent penalty on an unpaid first half after its due date, and a like 10 percent on the balance of unpaid current taxes after the second-half date, under R.C. 323.121.

faqs.q: Does the homestead exemption move to the buyer of my house?
faqs.a: No. It applies to a qualifying owner who lives in the home, and the auditor requires ownership changes to be reported. A buyer has to qualify and apply on their own.
